text: Okay. Thanks, Christie. Okay. So next slide, please. So my name is Ben LaHaze. I'm the founder of Community Fiber Company. The company was founded back in 2013. Its origins back in 2005, when I moved back to the Leinark Highlands area after living in Toronto for a number of years. I sort of had the same problem everybody else has with connectivity. I've worked remotely as a software developer for a large part of my career and having decent internet at home has been vital to being able to work remotely. Community Fiber has a mission is to address the rural broadband gaps that we have using fiber. So we have about 85 kilometers of network coverage right now. It's a good chunk in out in Leinark Highlands around Patterson Lake and parts part of Dalhousie Lake. The bigger part of our customers are around the Ashton area, around, along Flewellyn, Dwyer Hill, Fernbank. We have coverage out on Kidd Road. What else? Parts of Beckwith Ninth Line and all that sort of area back in there. And right now we have, there are sort of three parts to our network. The one that served out in the Ashton area from our pop on Dwyer Hill. We have another pocket of about 50, some 52 customers over on John Asselford and Marchurst where a subdivision that had been trouble, having trouble getting any service in contracted us to go on and put in service for our residents there. And then our other part of the network out here in Leinark Highlands, McDonald's Corners and a couple other pockets on Crampton Road out in Innisfil and a few customers over on Wolf Grove Road near Elmont. Next slide please. So, oh yes, yeah. We have more than 90 kilometers of fiber coverage. Most of the network uses a technology called passive optical networking where one fiber can service a number of homes. It's currently providing speeds of up to one gigabit or 1000 megabits and it's all fiber so it is scalable. Higher speeds in the future will only require swapping out the electronics at the end. Fiber connections we have from Dwyer Hill and Marchurst go back to a data center over in 436 Hazeldene. And because we have a fully fiber network, all of our packages are unlimited usage so people don't have to worry about overages and their monthly fees. Next slide please. Right now we have a project that I'm not entirely able to say who is helping fund yet because we don't have that approval that is enabling us to build some expansion out around the prospect area in Beckwith. And part of that includes a connection and a new pop that will be over on McLaughlin Road where the rail trail intersects with McLaughlin. And so as a result of that work, we will have fiber coming down Beckwith Boundary Road as well as the fiber going into McLaughlin. And I would like to go and add on a portion in Montague along Pinery that has sort of two benefits. One is that we would be able to serve the approximately 83 homes that are along Pinery Road. And the other benefit is that it would allow us to add another redundant path between the Beckwith Boundary Road and the McLaughlin pop. So the map that's on the right-hand side there has sort of three segments to it. Two of them are red, which would be aerial builds on existing telephone poles. And then there's the section in between where there's no pole line along Pinery that's around 1.82 kilometers. I don't know the exact number there where we would like to go and bury a fiber optic cable along Pinery Road to go and connect those two segments together. Next slide, please. Benefits is that the 83 homes on Pinery will gain full fiber to the home services. So they'll be able to get speeds the same as elsewhere in the Ashton network with gigabit. It will no longer be underserved. So I know some homes can get a little bit of DSL on the side of Pinery that's closer to Highway 15, but the majority of it, there's no fiber out there and folks have to be on either wireless or satellite. One of the benefits of fiber deployments, there have been a number of studies that have reported increased value for home sales in the neighborhood of anywhere to five to $6,000 from some of the studies that have been made. And increasingly what we've found in a lot of the areas around here is people are making, having a decent high-speed internet becomes a requirement for home sales to go through. So we regularly get calls from potential home buyers to check in and make sure that service is actually available in Beckwith and other parts of the network. Yes, aerial coverage for most of Pinery Road is going to be cost-effective. So part of the project that we're doing in the prospect area and McLaughlin is to demonstrate a particular way of construction that lets us go and roll out fiber in a bit of a faster, lower cost sort of method. And part of the way that this form of construction works is that we have redundant paths. So each home that's on the network gains the ability to get service from either sort of East or West as it's referred to in networks. And this allows us to use a particular construction style that is more cost-effective and faster. Next slide, please. So our request from Montague Township is we would like to have a municipal consent in order to install the buried section along Pinery Road. I understand from talking to staff that it will be necessary to go and relocate the cable when that part of Pinery Road is widened next year. I'm entirely okay with that because part of the benefit of that network construction is that even if that cable gets cut or severed, it doesn't matter. The customers will be able to remain online even if construction goes and damages the cable. The other part is we will be using a fairly low cost network in the short term on that segment just because of the construction that will be happening next year. And as part of that, we're willing to waive all liability for damage to the cable from normal operations like grading of the road or snow removal. And yeah, the only sort of ask that we have is we need to move a little bit quickly in order to get it done before the ground goes and freezes in the coming months. Next slide.
